Adult Fat snook (Centropomus parallelus) are known to attain a substantial ultimate total length of 72 centimeters [Li = 72 centimeters], a size that distinguishes them from several smaller congeners found in nearshore habitats. Reaching such an impressive adult body size requires a prolonged growth phase, during which individuals must navigate seasonal shifts in prey availability within estuarine environments. The species exhibits a clear size threshold for the onset of reproductive capability, with puberty occurring once individuals achieve a total length of 36 centimeters [Lp = 36 centimeters]. This dimension serves as a critical biological benchmark, as individuals below this length are generally incapable of initiating gonadal recrudescence and remain in a juvenile, non-reproductive state. Field surveys indicate that most fish in a given cohort surpass this pubertal length during their second or third year of life, though local variations in temperature and food supply can influence the precise timing of this developmental transition.

At the onset of reproductive activity, a female Fat snook typically attains a wet weight of 625 grams [Wwp = 625 grams], a mass that reflects the substantial energetic investment required to support vitellogenesis and the production of high-quality oocytes. This pubertal body mass is derived from the allometric relationship between length and weight, and it represents a point at which energy allocation begins to shift more heavily toward gamete production. In contrast, the maximum published weight for the species reaches an impressive 5,000 grams [Wwi = 5,000 grams], a value recorded from particularly large, aged individuals captured in productive mangrove-lined lagoons. Such an ultimate wet weight is indicative of a long-lived, iteroparous life history strategy, wherein individuals continue to grow slowly after reaching maturity and can achieve considerable bulk. The disparity between mass at puberty and ultimate mass underscores the extended period of somatic growth that characterizes this species, allowing females to produce progressively larger clutches as they age.

The earliest life stages of the Fat snook are characterized by a remarkably small initial body size, with the wet weight at birth calculated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams]. This minute mass corresponds to a pelagic egg with an approximate diameter of 0.8 millimeters, a common dimension for teleost eggs that undergo a period of planktonic drift following broadcast spawning. Incubation and early development proceed rapidly under stable thermal conditions; at a water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], larval emergence, or eclosion, occurs after only 20 days [ab = 20 days]. This relatively brief incubation period is characteristic of warm-water species and allows the yolk-sac larva to begin exogenous feeding before its limited endogenous reserves are fully exhausted. The combination of a tiny initial mass and a short time to hatching reflects a strategy that prioritizes rapid entry into the planktonic feeding environment over prolonged yolk dependency.

Under the same thermal regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], the species displays a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], placing it among the longer-lived members of the Centropomidae family. This extended longevity, which translates to roughly 5,475 days, permits multiple spawning seasons over a lifetime, a classic feature of an iteroparous reproductive strategy. Field studies using otolith microchemistry have confirmed that individuals can reach this advanced age in undisturbed habitats, though fishing pressure in many estuaries truncates the age structure considerably. The warm, stable temperature that supports rapid early development also appears to sustain the slow, steady metabolic processes that underpin somatic maintenance in adulthood, allowing these fish to avoid the rapid senescence seen in shorter-lived tropical species.

In terms of annual reproductive output, females produce roughly 2,500 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = roughly 2,500 eggs per spawning event], and multiple spawning events occur annually [F_R_i = multiple spawning events occur annually]. This translates into a very high maximum reproductive rate, reaching approximately 900,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 900,000 eggs per year] when considering the entire year under optimal conditions at 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. Such prolific egg production is a common adaptation among estuarine-dependent fishes that face high rates of early-life mortality, ensuring that at least a fraction of the offspring survive the hazardous planktonic phase. The combination of high fecundity, rapid early growth, and a long reproductive lifespan makes the Fat snook a resilient species capable of sustaining populations in dynamic coastal environments.
